standards: Career Education and Work – 13.3.11.F: Demonstrate appropriate work habits and behaviors.
Mathematics – PA Academic Standards: Students will apply mathematical concepts and skills to solve problems and interpret mathematical information in meaningful contexts.
essential_questions: Students will consider:
How can I use counting skills to solve a problem?
How can I compare numbers?
How can I follow a checklist to prepare for class?
How can I use technology to complete a math activity?
How can I practice being independent when using online programs?
objectives: By the end of the lesson, students will:
Follow the classroom beginning-of-class checklist with verbal and/or visual prompting as needed.
Participate in a five-minute mindfulness activity and review classroom expectations.
Demonstrate counting skills during the "What's the Number Wednesday" warm-up.
Group 1: Count squares on a graph and communicate the number counted using their AAC devices with teacher support as needed.
Group 2: Count squares on a graph and answer comparison questions, including identifying which number is greatest and which is smallest.
Access and log into IXL in preparation for the upcoming benchmark.
Access and log into Bankability in preparation for the first use of the program during the week.
Demonstrate appropriate participation and work behaviors during individual and small-group activities.
assessment: Following the beginning-of-class checklist.
Participating in mindfulness and classroom expectations.
Responding to the "What's the Number Wednesday" counting activity.
Using AAC devices to communicate answers when appropriate.
Verbally answering questions during the warm-up.
Demonstrating the ability to compare numbers for students working at that level.
Successfully logging into IXL.
Successfully logging into Bankability.
Following directions during transitions between activities.
Participating appropriately during small-group instruction.
differentiation: Group 1 – Foundational Skills / Intensive Communication Supports
Students in Group 1 use AAC devices to communicate.
Teacher uses both verbal language and her own AAC/talking device to model important vocabulary and directions.
For example, the teacher may verbally say "Go get your folder" while simultaneously selecting "folder" on her AAC device.
Teacher models functional communication such as "hello," "folder," "number," and other relevant vocabulary.
Students use their own AAC devices to communicate answers.
Counting activity focuses on counting the squares on a graph.
Students communicate the number they counted using their AAC devices.
Directions are presented in short, clear steps.
Students receive additional wait time for communication.
Teacher provides prompting as needed and allows students opportunities to respond independently.
Visual and verbal supports are provided throughout the lesson.
Group 2 – More Independent Learners
Students receive the same general directions but require fewer communication supports.
Students verbally answer questions.
During the counting activity, students count the squares and answer questions such as:
"Which number is biggest?"
"Which number is smallest?"
Students are encouraged to explain their answers when appropriate.
Students work toward greater independence when accessing IXL and Bankability.
Teacher provides prompts or assistance only when necessary.
For Both Groups
Students receive access to the same classroom routines.
Students receive individualized prompting based on their needs.
Students are provided opportunities to demonstrate independence before teacher assistance is given.
Expectations are adjusted to students' individual skill levels while maintaining participation in the same lesson.
environment: The classroom follows a predictable beginning-of-class routine to support organization, independence, and successful transitions.
When students enter:
Students refer to the checklist displayed on the board.
Students gather their required materials.
Students prepare their folders/materials for class.
Students participate in a five-minute mindfulness meditation.
Students review classroom expectations.
Students participate in the warm-up.
Students transition into small-group activities.
A positive reinforcement system is used throughout the lesson. Students earn a fake dollar bill when they answer questions, participate appropriately, or demonstrate positive classroom behaviors.
The teacher uses specific positive feedback to reinforce participation and effort.

For students who use AAC, the classroom environment supports multiple forms of communication. Students are given adequate time to use their devices and are not expected to respond verbally when AAC is their established communication method.
prior_knowledge: The lesson begins with the familiar classroom checklist. Students are prompted to gather their materials and prepare for class.

The teacher then leads a five-minute mindfulness meditation followed by a review of classroom expectations. This provides a predictable transition into academic instruction and prepares students for learning.

Students then participate in "What's the Number Wednesday," a familiar counting activity from News-2-You. Using a familiar routine helps activate previously practiced counting skills while allowing the teacher to differentiate the level of questions based on each group's needs.
Students are motivated through:
Familiar classroom routines
Interactive questioning
Use of AAC devices
Digital learning programs
Positive reinforcement using classroom fake dollar bills
Opportunities to demonstrate independence

sequence: Group 1 – Approximately 45 minutes
1. Arrival/Beginning-of-Class Routine – 5 minutes
Students enter the classroom.
Teacher directs students' attention to the checklist on the board.
Students gather their folders and other required materials.
Teacher provides verbal and visual/AAC support as needed.
Teacher models language using her AAC device alongside verbal directions.
Example:
Teacher says:
"Go get your folder."
Teacher simultaneously selects "folder" on her AAC device.
This provides students with both verbal language and an AAC model.
2. Mindfulness – 5 minutes
Students participate in a five-minute mindfulness meditation.
Teacher provides reminders and prompts as necessary.
Students transition to the academic portion of class.
3. Classroom Expectations – 3–5 minutes
Teacher reviews classroom expectations.
Students listen and/or respond to questions.
Students are reminded of the classroom reinforcement system.
Students can earn classroom dollar bills for participation and answering questions.
4. What's the Number Wednesday – Approximately 10 minutes
Teacher introduces the News-2-You counting activity.
Students count the squares on the graph.
Teacher provides prompts as needed.
Students use their AAC devices to communicate the number they counted.
Teacher models relevant math vocabulary through verbal language and AAC.
Students receive positive reinforcement for participation.
5. Small-Group/Digital Learning Activity – Approximately 15 minutes
Students are divided into smaller groups.
Group A:
Students practice logging into IXL in preparation for their upcoming benchmark.
Teacher supports students with:
Finding the website/program
Entering login information
Navigating to the appropriate area
Troubleshooting login issues
Increasing independence with the routine
Group B:
Students practice logging into Bankability in preparation for using the program later in the week.
Teacher supports students with:
Accessing the program
Logging in
Navigating the platform
Becoming familiar with the program
6. Groups Switch – Approximately 5 minutes
Students transition to the other digital learning activity.
Teacher provides transition reminders and prompts.
Students practice accessing the second program.
7.Anyone who finishes early can go back and play UNO with TA
Group 2 – Approximately 45 minutes
The same overall routine and lesson structure is used.
1. Beginning-of-Class Checklist – 5 minutes
Students:
Check the board.
Gather materials.
Get their folders.
Prepare for class.
Teacher encourages greater independence with the routine.
2. Mindfulness – 5 minutes
Students participate in the five-minute mindfulness activity.
3. Classroom Expectations – 3–5 minutes
Teacher reviews classroom expectations and reminds students about the classroom dollar reinforcement system.
4. What's the Number Wednesday – Approximately 10 minutes
Students complete the same News-2-You counting activity.
Students:
Count the squares on the graph.
Identify the number represented.
Answer comparison questions such as:
"Which number is biggest?"
"Which number is smallest?"
Teacher asks follow-up questions when appropriate and encourages students to explain their answers.
5. Small-Group/Digital Learning Activities – Approximately 15 minutes
Students are divided into smaller groups.
One group practices logging into IXL in preparation for the upcoming benchmark.
The other group practices logging into Bankability in preparation for using the program later in the week.
Teacher monitors students' ability to navigate each program and provides assistance as needed.
6. Groups Switch – Approximately 5 minutes
Students switch to the other digital learning activity.
Teacher monitors transitions and supports students in accessing the second program.
7.Anyone who finishes early can go back and play UNO with TA
closure: Ask questions such as:
"What did we practice today?"
"What number did you count?"
"Which number was the biggest?"
"Which number was the smallest?"
"What programs did we practice logging into?"
"What did you do when you needed help?"
Provide positive feedback for participation and effort.

lessons.title: Counting Dollars: Do I Have Enough?

standards: PA Academic Standards for Personal Finance, 17.3.9-12.A — Develop a process for making informed spending decisions, considering factors such as price and reliability of information.
PA Academic Standards for Personal Finance, 17.3.9-12.C — Develop a personal approach to keeping track of income and spending.
PA Academic Standards for Personal Finance, 17.3.9-12.D — Evaluate budgeting approaches and methods for organizing money.
Career Education and Work connections: students practice financial decision-making, responsibility, and life-readiness skills.
essential_questions: How can I use money responsibly?
How can I tell whether I have enough money to buy something?
Why is it important to keep track of money, spending, saving, and bills?
objectives: By the end of the lesson, students will:
Count a given amount of money using one-dollar bills with increasing independence.
Determine whether they have enough money to purchase a pictured/itemized product by comparing the amount they have with the cost.
Identify where money, bills, and spending information are located within Digitability/Bankability.
Demonstrate an understanding that money can be spent or saved for a future purchase.
Participate using speech, AAC, sign language, pointing, writing, or another established communication method.
Demonstrate the targeted skills with at least 80% accuracy, with IEP accommodations and prompting as needed.
assessment: Teacher observation during the money-counting warm-up.
Whiteboard responses showing the amount of money each student has.
Yes/No responses using AAC, speech, pointing, or another communication method when deciding whether the student has enough money for a product.
Teacher questioning during Digitability/Bankability review.
Observation of students locating their account balance, bills, shopping area, and saving/spending options.
Completion/progress within IXL as an additional individualized math practice measure.
closure: questions in which students identify one money skill learned or demonstrate a related routine.
differentiation: Provide AAC devices and model functional vocabulary such as “cost,” “money,” “buy,” “save,” and “bank.”
Pair verbal directions with visual directions, gestures, modeling, and the posted visual schedule.
Provide clearly pictured products and one-dollar bills for students who benefit from concrete materials.
Allow students to point, gesture, use AAC, sign, write, or verbally respond.
Reduce the number of choices/items when needed and provide one-step directions.
Use least-to-most prompting and fade prompts when students demonstrate independence.
Provide adult assistance with counting or writing when required by the student’s IEP.
Allow extended time and repeated practice.
Use the FM device and preferential positioning as appropriate.
Use a calculator or other established math accommodation when appropriate and consistent with the student’s IEP.
For students demonstrating mastery, increase the amount of money, introduce multiple items, or ask them to explain whether they should spend or save.
IXL and Digitability activities may be individualized to each student’s instructional level.
environment: Students will enter, read the visual schedule, collect their math materials, and sit in their appropriate work area.
The teacher will greet each student individually and use the AAC device to model a functional greeting.
Students will review classroom expectations at the beginning of each instructional block.
The posted visual schedule and timers will communicate transitions and reduce uncertainty.
Students will receive specific positive reinforcement for following routines, participating, communicating, and completing tasks.
During the class switch, the second group will have a predictable snack and break routine before beginning instruction.
Students may use established regulation supports, such as a brief break, appropriate fidgets, or a quiet work location, as needed and consistent with classroom plans.
Adults will use calm, concise directions and consistent language.
Students will be prompted to return to the task after breaks using the visual schedule/timer.
All students will have access to materials and communication supports so that physical or communication needs do not prevent participation.
prior_knowledge: Preparing students for the lesson
Begin with the familiar Money Monday routine and connect the lesson to students’ previous experience with Digitability/Bankability.
Ask students what money is used for and allow responses through speech, AAC, pointing, signs, or gestures.
Show pictured grocery items and ask students to predict whether a given amount of money is enough.
Explain that today’s activities practice everyday skills such as shopping, saving money, checking an account, and paying bills.
materials: Math folders, laptops, whiteboard, whiteboard markers, projection screen, math slide show, visual schedule, AAC device, FM device, timers, fake dollar bills, IXL program
vocabulary: Bankability, Digitability, Cost, Amount, Budget, Bills, Deposit, Savings, Shop, Spend, Bank
sequence: 0–5 minutes — Entry-Let the kids read the schedule on the board, grab their math materials and sit in their seats, use the AAC device to say hello to all students individually, reward students with cash when they get their folders

5–12 minutes — Start the morning mindfulness video once all students have their materials and are ready to start. After mindfulness, students will read the expectations. They will raise their hand and share an expectation on their AAC device, pass them reward money as they do this. Use AAC device to help them as needed. Show them the math sign language for the week: “cost.” Demonstrate how to sign “cost” and allow the students to try as well. Play the quick video that also shows the kids how to sign “cost.”

12-22 minutes — Warm -Up: Money Monday- Show a video “Money 101”. After the video finishes, hand students dollar bills to use for the warm-up. They will need their white boards and markers as well. Give one student 5 dollars, one student 3 dollars, one student 4 dollars and one student 2 dollars. Have the student count the money they were given and write it on their white board (or have an adult write it as needed). We will then look at 4 different grocery store products and ask the kids if they have enough for the products. (Yes or No on AAC device)

22–34 minutes — Whole Group Lesson on Digitability: Allow students to login to their digitability accounts. They have all used this program before so it will be a review on where to find their bills/bank account information/ where to shop, etc. We will first look at where they can see how much is in their account and they can see if they have money left over from last year. We will also discuss the bills that they will pay throughout the school year and when they will pay them. Make sure to give the students a reminder that they can save their money or they can use it to stop every week. If they want a bigger prize they will need to save their money until they can afford it.

35–48 minutes — Classes switch, second group comes in and looks at the schedule on the board. They will grab their math materials and sit down for snack time. After they have their snack, they have break time where they can sit anywhere in the room and do any activity of their choice. There will be a timer on the board that tells them when to get back to their seat for class time.

48–55 minutes — Start the morning mindfulness video once all students have their materials and are ready to start. After mindfulness, students will read the expectations. They will raise their hand and share an expectation, pass them reward money as they do this. Show them the math sign language for the week: “cost.” Demonstrate how to sign “cost” and allow the students to try as well. Play the quick video that also shows the kids how to sign “cost.”
55–65 minutes — Warm -Up: Money Monday- Show a video “Money 101”. Explain why _____

65–85 minutes – Allow students to finish their IXL benchmarks, when/if students are finished, they can come to the back table and login to their digitability accounts. They have all used this program before so it will be a review on where to find their bills/bank account information/ where to shop, etc. We will first look at where they can see how much is in their account and they can see if they have money left over from last year. We will also discuss the bills that they will pay throughout the school year and when they will pay them. Make sure to give the students a reminder that they can save their money or they can use it to stop every week. If they want a bigger prize they will need to save their money until they can afford it.
80–90 minutes — Closure/Review: Review digitability/bankability rules/expectations with students and allow them a 5 minute-break for working so hard
Closure:

Review the students’ Bankability/Digitability expectations and ask each student to identify or demonstrate one money skill from the lesson. Reinforce the importance of knowing how much money is available, understanding the cost of an item, and deciding whether to spend or save. Remind students of the routine for coming to the “bank” and depositing money and review when bills are due. Preview that the next lesson will build on these skills through additional functional money activities.

How can counting and recognizing numbers help me in everyday life
objectives: By the end of the lesson, students will:
Demonstrate one-to-one counting by counting numbers in sequence during the dot-to-dot activity.
Identify and connect numbers in the correct numerical order.
Follow a turn-taking routine by connecting three dots before allowing the next student to participate.
Answer teacher questions about the picture created by the dot-to-dot activity.

Teacher observation of students counting and identifying numbers during the dot-to-dot warm-up.
Observation of students connecting the correct three dots in numerical sequence.
Student responses to questions about the completed picture, such as what the picture is, how many objects they see, or what numbers they connected.
Teacher observation of communication, turn-taking, attention to task, and independence.
IXL progress-monitoring data collected by the TA.

Use the 1–36 city dot-to-dot for the second group to provide increased numerical range and challenge.
Break the task into manageable turns of three dots at a time.

Allow additional time for students who need it to locate and connect the correct number.

materials: Math folders, laptops, whiteboard, whiteboard markers, projection screen, math slideshow/visual examples, visual schedule, AAC devices, FM device as applicable, first-group 1–10 car dot-to-dot, second-group 1–36 city dot-to-dot, classroom timer, dollar bills/fake dollar bills for participation, IXL, Digitability, and UNO cards.
vocabulary: Number, count, counting, sequence, number order, before, after, next, dot, connect, picture, quantity, more, less, turn, city, car.
sequence: 0–5 minutes — Entry Routine: Students enter, check the visual schedule, collect materials, and sit in their work area. Teacher greets students individually. With the first group, teacher uses AAC to model greetings and functional communication. Dollar bills are provided for participation and completion of the entry routine.

5–10 minutes — Mindfulness/Expectations: Complete the usual mindfulness routine. Review classroom expectations and allow students to participate using speech, AAC, gestures, or another established method. Provide longer processing time for the first group.

10–25 minutes — What’s the Number Wednesday Warm-Up, First Group: Display the 1–10 dot-to-dot car picture on the whiteboard. Review the numbers and explain that students will connect the dots in numerical order to reveal the picture. Students come to the board one at a time and connect three dots. The next student then connects the next three dots. Continue until the picture is completed. Teacher supports students with counting, number identification, and sequencing as needed. Students waiting for their turn remain engaged by watching for the next number. Use AAC and extended processing time for communication. Provide dollar bills for participation and effort.

25–35 minutes — Picture Questions/Review: After the car is completed, ask students questions about their drawing. Questions may include: “What did we make?”, “What number did you connect?”, “What number comes next?”, and “How many numbers did we use?” Students respond using speech, AAC, pointing, gestures, or another established method. Teacher provides feedback and reteaches number sequence when needed.

35–45 minutes — Snack and Break/Transition: Students clean up, transition according to the visual schedule, and participate in snack. Students then have a short break and may choose an appropriate activity. The timer signals when students should return.

45–50 minutes — Second Group Entry Routine: Second group enters, checks the visual schedule, gathers materials, and completes the snack/break routine as needed. Teacher reviews expectations and provides dollar bills for appropriate participation.

50–55 minutes — Mindfulness/Counting Review: Complete the usual mindfulness routine and briefly review counting and number order. Count together and explain that today’s activity will use numbers 1–36.

55–70 minutes — What’s the Number Wednesday Warm-Up, Second Group: Display the 1–36 city dot-to-dot on the whiteboard. Explain that students will work together to connect the numbers in numerical order. Students come to the board one at a time and connect three dots, then the next student connects the following three. Continue until the city picture is completed. Teacher monitors number identification, counting, sequencing, and appropriate turn-taking.

sequence: 0–5 minutes — Entry Routine

Display picture patterns on the board. Students examine each pattern and choose what comes next. Teacher models the first example by identifying what repeats or changes. Students take turns responding. Students may come to the board, point to an answer, verbally respond, use AAC, or use another established communication method. Review the patterns and ask questions such as: What comes next? What picture repeats? How did you know? Which answer does not belong? Encourage students to explain or demonstrate their reasoning at their individual communication level.

standards: This lesson addresses Pennsylvania mathematics standards through functional application of mathematical skills, including telling time, interpreting data presented in graphs, comparing quantities, addition, and using money. The lesson also incorporates functional communication, independence, and transition-related skills.
essential_questions:   How can I use a clock to understand and communicate time?
  How can I use a pictograph to understand information?
  How can I use math skills in real-life situations?
objectives:   Demonstrate understanding of time by modeling a given time on a Judy clock.
  Identify the hour and minute hands on an analog clock.
  Answer questions about time based on their individual instructional level.
  Interpret information presented in a pictograph by counting, comparing, and identifying quantities.
  Communicate mathematical answers using AAC devices, verbal responses, pointing, or other established communication methods as appropriate.
  Group 2 students will practice determining what a clock will look like after 30 minutes have passed.
  Students completing IXL will work on their individualized recommended math skills.
  The student completing the time-card activity will practice recording time worked and calculating money earned as a functional workplace/office skill.
assessment: Students will show what they know by:
Participating in the classroom routines and expectations.
Responding to teacher prompts using AAC devices or verbal communication.
Demonstrating the ASL sign of the week, "deposit," when able.
Modeling times on Judy clocks.
Identifying the hour and minute hands.
Answering questions about what happens when 30 minutes pass.
Answering questions based on pictographs.
Completing individualized IXL recommendations.
Completing the time-card and money calculation activity.
Teacher observation, questioning, prompting, and review of student work will be used as ongoing formative assessment.
differentiation: Group 1:

Students will receive AAC modeling throughout the lesson. The teacher will use an AAC device to greet students, give directions, model vocabulary, and communicate when appropriate. Students will receive additional processing time, repeated directions, visual supports, modeling, prompting, and hands-on materials such as Judy clocks. Pictograph questions will be adjusted to each student's individual instructional level. Students may answer through their AAC device, verbally, by pointing, or through another established communication method.
Group 2:

Students will receive more opportunities for independent work and higher-level questioning. Students will practice telling time to the half hour and reasoning about elapsed time. Students will work on individualized IXL recommendations based on their needs.
environment: A visual schedule will be projected on the whiteboard when students enter the classroom. The schedule will identify the activities for the day as well as the materials students will need. Students will be prompted as needed to gather their materials.

The classroom follows a consistent routine to help students understand expectations and transitions. Group 1 will begin with materials, mindfulness, classroom expectations, the ASL sign of the week, the Time Tuesday warm-up, and the day's math activity.
Group 1 students will receive AAC modeling throughout the lesson. The teacher will model appropriate AAC use while also providing students with opportunities to use their own devices.
Group 2 will begin with snack and a 10-minute leisure break before beginning the instructional routine.

Fake money will be provided throughout the warm-up as positive reinforcement for participation and following classroom expectations. The teacher will use positive reinforcement, prompting, visual supports, redirection, wait time, and individual assistance to support student engagement and independence.
prior_knowledge: The projected visual schedule will prepare students for the activities they will complete during class. The consistent classroom routine will help students anticipate the sequence of activities.
The Time Tuesday warm-up will activate students' previous knowledge of telling time and using an analog clock. Students will use hands-on Judy clocks to physically model different times.
For Group 1, the teacher will model time on a Judy clock and students will copy the time on their own clocks. Students will then identify which picture matches the time shown.

For Group 2, students will independently demonstrate a time on their Judy clocks and identify the hour and minute hands. The teacher will extend the activity by asking what the clock would look like if 30 minutes passed.
The use of fake money during participation provides additional motivation and reinforcement.

sequence: Group 1 — 45 Minutes
1. Entry Routine and Materials
Approx. 0–5 minutes
The visual schedule and materials needed for the day will be projected on the whiteboard as students enter.
Students will be prompted to gather their materials.
Teacher will greet students using the AAC device.
Teacher will use the AAC device to tell students to get their materials.
AAC modeling will continue throughout the lesson when appropriate.
2. Mindfulness
Approx. 5–10 minutes
Students will participate in a mindfulness meditation video.
Teacher will provide prompts as needed to help students attend to the activity.
3. Classroom Expectations
Approx. 10–15 minutes
Teacher will review the classroom expectations.
Students will have the opportunity to communicate the expectations using their AAC devices.
Teacher will provide assistance, modeling, and wait time as needed.
Students who are able may verbally state expectations.
4. ASL Sign of the Week
Approx. 15–18 minutes
Teacher will introduce the ASL sign of the week: "deposit."
Teacher will model the sign.
Students will attempt the sign if they are able.
5. Time Tuesday Warm-Up
Approx. 18–28 minutes
Teacher will model a time using the teacher Judy clock.
Students will use their own Judy clocks to model the same time.
Teacher will display pictures showing different times.
Students will identify which picture matches the time on their clock.
Students may answer using AAC devices, speech, pointing, or another established response method.
Teacher will provide fake money as students participate and follow classroom expectations.
Teacher will provide additional prompts and modeling as needed.
6. Pictograph Practice
Approx. 28–45 minutes
Teacher will introduce a pictograph.
Students will examine the pictures and information shown on the graph.
Questions will be differentiated according to individual student ability.
Some students may:
Count the pictures.
Identify how many items are represented.
Identify which group has more.
Identify which group has less.
Compare two quantities.
Answer simple questions about the graph.
Students will use their AAC devices to communicate answers when appropriate.
Teacher will model relevant vocabulary using AAC.
Teacher will provide wait time, prompts, and feedback.
Teacher will monitor individual student understanding throughout the activity.
Group 2 — 45 Minutes
1. Snack and Leisure Break
Approx. 0–10 minutes
Students will enter and have their snack.
Students will participate in a 10-minute leisure break.
Students in this group are generally more independent and do not use AAC devices as their primary communication system.
2. Mindfulness
Approx. 10–15 minutes
Students will participate in the mindfulness meditation video.
Teacher will provide reminders and prompts as needed.
3. Classroom Expectations
Approx. 15–20 minutes
Teacher will review the classroom expectations.
Students will identify or discuss the expectations.
Teacher will reinforce appropriate participation and classroom behavior.
4. ASL Sign of the Week
Approx. 20–23 minutes
Teacher will introduce and model the ASL sign "deposit."
Students will practice the sign if they are able.
5. Time Tuesday Warm-Up
Approx. 23–33 minutes
Teacher will display a time on the board.
Students will read the time and demonstrate it on their Judy clocks.
Students will identify what the hour hand is pointing to.
Students will identify what the minute hand is pointing to.
Teacher will ask questions such as:
"What time is it?"
"Which hand is the hour hand?"
"Which hand is the minute hand?"
"What would it look like if 30 minutes passed?"
Students will adjust their clocks to demonstrate the new time.
Teacher will check each student's understanding and provide feedback.
6. Individualized Math Practice
Approx. 33–45 minutes
Students completing IXL:
Students will log into IXL.
Students will work on their individualized recommended skills.
Teacher will circulate and provide assistance.
Teacher will monitor student progress and provide prompts or reteaching when needed.
Student completing the time-card activity:
This student will work with classmates' time cards.
Student will determine how much time each classmate worked.
Student will add the amount of time worked.
Student will calculate how much money the classmates earned.
Teacher will provide prompts and check calculations.
This activity will provide practice with:
Time
Addition
Money
Record keeping
Following a workplace procedure
Office-related skills
This activity is connected to the student's goal of eventually working in an office environment and provides a meaningful opportunity to practice a functional workplace task.
closure: At the end of each 45-minute group, the teacher will briefly review the main skill practiced during the lesson.
Group 1:
Students will identify or demonstrate something they practiced with time or pictographs.
Students may communicate their response using AAC, speech, pointing, or another established method.
Group 2:
Students will demonstrate a time on their Judy clock or answer a question about what happens when 30 minutes pass.
Students may also briefly discuss what they practiced on IXL or during the time-card activity.
Teacher will reinforce participation, communication, and independence and will use the visual schedule to help students transition to the next activity or class.

Model all communication using classroom AAC device; accept any modality (AAC, gesture, pointing, eye gaze, sign).
Provide physical prompting, hand-over-hand support, or adult scribing for deposit slips.
Use least-to-most prompting; fade when student shows independence.
Pair verbal directions with visual supports, gestures, and modeling.
TA, PCAs, and cooperating teacher provide 1:1 support during banking rotation.
Reduce money denominations or total amount based on individual skill level.
GROUP 2 (more independent / verbal):
Students count money and complete deposit slips independently before coming to the bank.
Students use calculators to add item costs and determine affordability.
Extend: ask students to calculate change or compare prices of multiple items.
Students verbally explain their banking decisions (deposit, save, or spend).
BOTH GROUPS:
Visual schedules and timers communicate transitions.
Positive reinforcement for following routines and participating.
Extended time as needed per IEP.
FM device and preferential seating as appropriate per IEP.
— Behavior Management Plan & Routines
Students enter, locate their math folder and deposit slip at their workstation, and follow the posted visual schedule.
Student teacher greets Group 1 individually using the AAC device to model "hello"; Group 2 receives a verbal greeting.
Classroom expectations are reviewed at the start of each block; banking routine is previewed.
A visual schedule and countdown timer are posted and referenced throughout both blocks.
Cooperating teacher, TA, and PCAs circulate during the banking rotation to minimize wait time for Group 1.
Positive verbal and tangible reinforcement (reward cash) is provided for following routines and communicating.
Group 1: Classroom is arranged for wheelchair/mobility access; AAC devices are charged and available at each workstation.
Group 2: Students have a 10-minute snack/leisure break upon arrival before independent work begins.
Cool Math Games serves as a structured independent activity after banking is complete.
All adults use calm, consistent language and prompting strategies aligned with each student's IEP.
prior_knowledge: How will you activate prior knowledge, build background, or review previous lessons?
Students have participated in Bankability throughout the school year and are familiar with earning and depositing money.
They have practiced counting dollar bills in previous Life Skills Math lessons.
Prior lessons have introduced vocabulary: "deposit," "bank account," "balance," and "bills."
Activation for Group 1: Using the AAC device and visuals, ask "What do we do on Bankability day?" during the greeting routine.
Activation for Group 2: Brief verbal exchange during entry — "What do we do on Bankability day?" and "What does it mean to deposit money?"
materials: Earned cash (one-dollar bills and/or coins collected throughout the week)
Bankability computer program (student laptops + teacher computer)
vocabulary: Deposit, Withdrawal, Balance, Bank Account, Paycheck, Bills, Budget, Save, Spend, Cost, Afford, Receipt
sequence: Learning activities/strategies, student application, monitoring of performance:
── GROUP 1 (approx. 0–45 min) ──
0–5 min | Entry & Setup

Students enter and are assisted by TA/PCAs in locating their math folder and a deposit slip. Student teacher uses the AAC device to individually model "hello" to each student, accepting any communicative response. Visual schedule is reviewed.
5–10 min | Count Money & Fill Out Deposit Slip

Each student (with adult support as needed) counts earned cash using least-to-most prompting. Students write or have an adult scribe the total on their deposit slip. AAC device models functional vocabulary: "count," "money," "deposit," "how much."
10–40 min | Individual Banking Rotation
Student teacher calls students to the bank (teacher desk/computer) one at a time. At the bank:
Student teacher and student count the money together to verify the total.
Student teacher enters the deposit into Bankability and adds the weekly $100 paycheck.
Student teacher tells the student their new balance and whether any bills are due.
If the student has enough money after bills, they may shop at the school store, communicating their choice via AAC, pointing, or gesture.
While waiting, students are supported by TA/PCAs with deposit slips, quiet tasks, or regulation supports. Cool Math Games is available as a structured wait activity.
40–45 min | Closure & Transition (Group 1)

Student teacher briefly reviews: "Today we made a deposit and checked our balance." Each student is prompted to indicate one banking action (via AAC, gesture, or verbal). Students earn reward cash for participation. Group 1 transitions out.
── TRANSITION (approx. 45–55 min) ──
Group 2 enters and locates their math folder and a deposit slip. Students begin a 10-minute snack and leisure break. Timer is posted. Student teacher and TA reset the banking station.
── GROUP 2 (approx. 55–90 min) ──
55–65 min | Independent Money Counting & Deposit Slip Completion

After the break timer ends, students sit at workstations. Student teacher briefly reviews: "What are we doing today?" Students independently count earned cash and complete their deposit slip (name, date, amount). Student teacher circulates to check accuracy.
65–85 min | Individual Banking Rotation
Student teacher calls students to the bank one at a time. At the bank:
Student states: "I would like to make a deposit."
Student teacher and student count the money together to verify the deposit slip amount.
Student teacher enters the deposit and weekly $100 paycheck into Bankability.
Student teacher informs the student of their new balance and any bills due.
If the student wishes to shop, they use a calculator to add item costs and confirm affordability before purchasing.
Students not yet at the bank work independently: finishing deposit slips, calculating potential purchases from the school store price list, or playing Cool Math Games.
85–90 min | Closure (Group 2)

Student teacher brings group together. Students share one thing they did in Bankability today (e.g., "I made a deposit," "I paid a bill," "I saved my money"). Student teacher previews next Bankability day and reminds students to keep earning cash throughout the week.
Closure:
How will you bring closure to the lesson and preview what follows?
Group 1: Student teacher asks each student (via AAC, gesture, or verbal prompt) to indicate one banking action they completed. Reward cash given for participation.
Group 2: Students verbally share one thing they did in Bankability. Financial vocabulary is reinforced.
Both groups: Student teacher previews the next lesson, students will continue earning cash and have another opportunity to deposit and shop on the next Bankability day.
Students are reminded to keep track of their earnings during the week.

"Third, we decide how much we are going to PAY."

"Last, we CHECK our answer."

Pencil = $1

Teacher:

"What is our first step?"
"Do we need to add?"
"How much are you paying?"
"What operation should we use?"

Developing Group
Students will:

More Independent Group
Students will:

Calculate change.
Work with dollars and cents.

The teacher will circulate, monitor student performance, provide appropriate prompts, and document student progress.
40–45 Minutes —
closure: and Exit Ticket
The teacher will bring the lesson to a close by reviewing the five steps.
Teacher Script:
"Before we finish, who can tell me our five steps?"
Students will identify:
LOOK → ADD → PAY → SUBTRACT → CHECK
The teacher will then provide each student with one individualized exit-ticket problem.
Example:
A notebook costs $3.
You pay with $5.
How much change should you receive?
Students may answer by:

Using play money.
Using a calculator.
Pointing to the correct answer.
Verbally responding.
Demonstrating the transaction.

Preview of Next Lesson

Closure:
The lesson will conclude with students reviewing the five-step process:
LOOK → ADD → PAY → SUBTRACT → CHECK
Students will demonstrate their understanding through an individualized exit ticket.

The teacher will use student performance to determine whether the class is ready to progress to budgeting and more complex purchasing situations or whether additional instruction on identifying money, adding prices, or calculating change is needed.

lessons.title: Ordering Numbers, Absolute Value & Order of Operations

standards: Pennsylvania Academic Standards for Mathematics Algebra/Numbers and Quantities: students apply numerical reasoning, operations, and properties of real numbers. This lesson specifically addresses comparing/ordering real numbers, absolute value, and evaluating numerical expressions using the order of operations.
essential_questions: How can I use absolute value and the order of operations to accurately solve and compare mathematical expressions?
How do I know which number is greater when numbers are written in different forms? Why does the order of operations matter when solving an expression?
objectives: By the end of the lesson, students will: (1) sequence a set of numbers from least to greatest, including fractions, decimals, whole numbers, and square roots, using a calculator as needed; (2) determine the absolute value of a number and explain that it represents distance from zero; and (3) use the order of operations (PEMDAS) to evaluate numerical expressions accurately, using a calculator to check computations.
assessment: Students will show what they know by: completing the ordering-numbers warm-up with their table group; responding to teacher questions during guided notes and examples; solving practice examples on their calculators; completing an independent absolute-value maze worksheet; completing an independent order-of-operations color-by-number worksheet; and, if time permits, participating in a Blooket review. Teacher will circulate, question students, check calculator work, and provide immediate feedback
differentiation: Modifications in instruction and assessment for students with learning differences, specifically those with 504’s and IEP’s. Provide fill-in-the-blank notes, explicit modeling, chunked directions, repeated directions/check-ins, calculator access, extended time as needed, teacher/peer support during the group warm-up, reduced problem sets or selected problems when indicated by an IEP, and opportunities to demonstrate understanding orally or through guided work. Allow students to use familiar calculator procedures and visual reminders for PEMDAS. Extensions/Enrichment: students who demonstrate mastery may explain their strategy to a peer, compare multiple forms of the same number, or complete additional challenge expressions.
environment: Students will enter, collect/use the provided warm-up materials, and begin the ordering-numbers activity with their table group. Expectations will be stated before the activity: work cooperatively, handle number cards appropriately, use calculators responsibly, explain thinking, and remain engaged. During direct instruction, students will follow along with the fill-in-the-blank notes and participate when called on. During independent practice, students will work quietly, ask for help when needed, and remain on the assigned task. Teacher will circulate throughout the room, reinforce appropriate participation, redirect off-task behavior, and provide proximity and individual support as needed.
prior_knowledge: Begin with a collaborative ordering-numbers challenge. Students will receive individual number cards containing numbers in different forms (including whole numbers, decimals, fractions, and square roots) and work with their table group to arrange them from smallest to largest. Students may use calculators to determine decimal approximations and compare values. After groups finish, the class will discuss the sequence and explain how they determined the order. This activates prior knowledge of number sense, comparing values, decimals, fractions, and calculator use while creating a meaningful transition into absolute value and numerical expressions.
materials: Printed number cards cut into individual squares; calculators; fill-in-the-blank guided notes; pencils; absolute-value maze worksheet; order-of-operations color-by-number worksheet; Blooket (if time permits); teacher computer/projector as applicable.
vocabulary: absolute value, distance from zero, positive, negative, opposite, expression, operation, order of operations, PEMDAS, parentheses, exponent, multiplication, division, addition, subtraction, least to greatest.
sequence: 0–8 minutes — Entry/Ordering Numbers Warm-Up: Students enter and work with their table group to arrange the provided number cards from smallest to largest. Cards may include whole numbers, decimals, fractions, and square roots. Students use calculators as needed. Teacher circulates, observes strategies, asks questions, and supports students who need help comparing values.

8–15 minutes — Class Review of Warm-Up: Review the sequence as a class. Ask students how they compared fractions, decimals, square roots, and whole numbers. Address misconceptions and model calculator strategies when helpful. Connect the activity to the day's objective of accurately working with numbers and expressions.

15–25 minutes — Absolute Value Guided Notes: Distribute the fill-in-the-blank notes. Introduce absolute value as the distance of a number from zero on a number line. Complete the notes together and model several examples. Ask students to predict answers before checking them on their calculators.

25–35 minutes — Guided Absolute-Value Practice: Work through several absolute-value examples with students. Students enter examples into their calculators and record answers in their notes. Use questioning such as: 'What is the distance from zero?' and 'What happens when the number is negative?' Check for understanding before moving on.

35–45 minutes — Order of Operations Introduction: Transition to order of operations. Briefly review PEMDAS and explain why operations must be completed in the correct order. Model how to identify the first operation to complete and how to work through an expression step by step.

45–55 minutes — Guided Order-of-Operations Examples: Complete several examples together. Students solve along with the teacher using their notes and calculators to check computations. Pause after each major step to ask students what should be completed next and why.

55–65 minutes — Independent Guided Examples: Students complete the remaining examples independently on their calculators. Teacher circulates, checks work, asks individual students to explain their steps, and reteaches or models a problem when needed. Review answers with the class before independent worksheets.

65–80 minutes — Independent Practice: Students complete two practice activities: an absolute-value maze and an order-of-operations color-by-number worksheet. Students work independently while the teacher circulates, provides feedback, and checks for understanding. Students may use calculators and their guided notes.
80–90 minutes —
closure: /Review: Review selected problems from the worksheets and ask students to identify one strategy they used for absolute value and one strategy they used for order of operations. If time permits, finish with a short Blooket review using questions on absolute value and order of operations. If the Blooket cannot be completed, use a brief verbal/exit-ticket review instead.
Closure:

Bring the lesson together by revisiting the essential question. Ask students: ‘How do you feel about what we learned today?’, 'What does absolute value tell us?' and 'Why do we need to follow the order of operations?'

IEP/504: Accommodations in each student’s IEP/504 plan will be followed (for example, extra time or chunked directions).
Extension: Early finishers move on to their IXL recommendations.
environment: A visual schedule and a list of materials to grab are on the board when students enter, so routines are clear before class begins.
Students gather whiteboards, markers, erasers, and calculators during the first 5 minutes to settle in.
Students answer on whiteboards during the warm-up, and I invite volunteers to share the next step.
Small groups are split by readiness, with one group working with me and the other with my cooperating teacher.
After lunch, students choose their own seats as long as they are working. I circulate to help.
Early finishers work on their IXL recommendations or on unfinished work.
The class ends with a Halloween Gimkit celebration.
prior_knowledge: The warm-up reviews the steps for solving multistep equations that students already know. Students answer on whiteboards and are invited to say the next step, so they stay actively involved. Working in small groups at the same pace lets each student build confidence. The color-by-number and the Halloween Gimkit make the practice fun and motivating.
materials: Whiteboards, dry-erase markers, erasers, calculators, visual schedule and materials list (on the board), 4 warm-up multistep equations, multistep equation color-by-number, coloring supplies, pencils, student devices for IXL and Gimkit, Halloween Gimkit
vocabulary: Equation; variable; constant; coefficient; inverse operation; isolate; solution; check

Students read the visual schedule and materials list on the board.
Students grab whiteboards, markers, erasers, and calculators and settle in.
Whole-Class Warm-Up — 10 minutes
We solve 4 multistep equations together on the board.
I go through each step aloud and give students a chance to tell me the next step or the answer.
Students follow along on their whiteboards so I can see who understands and who needs support.
Small Group Instruction — 30 minutes
The class splits into 2 small groups by readiness, so students in each group work at a similar pace.
One group works with me and the other works with my cooperating teacher.
Students practice multistep equations, explaining steps and checking their work with teacher support.
Lunch
Independent Practice: Color-by-Number — after lunch
I hand out the multistep equation color-by-number.
Students work individually and may choose their own seat as long as they are working.
I circulate to help and check understanding.

Halloween Gimkit — end of class
The class plays a fun Halloween Gimkit as a small celebration.
closure: The class ends with a Halloween Gimkit that gives students one more chance to use their multistep equation skills while celebrating together. As students play, I can see which skills they know well and which need more practice.
Connection to Next Lesson: Teacher connects the lesson to continued practice solving multistep equations and checking solutions.

Solve multistep equations by carrying out each step in the correct order.
Show what they know about all three skills on a quiz.
assessment: Formative: Student participation in the whole-class warm-up.
Formative: Review worksheet, with my observation and help as I circulate.
Formative: Observation of partners during the distributive roll-a-dice game.

Process: I walk around the room to give help as each student needs it.

IEP/504: Accommodations in each student’s IEP/504 plan will be followed.
environment: Students begin with the warm-up on the whiteboard together.
Students work independently on the review while I circulate to help.
Students who finish the review hand it in and wait for everyone else, then play the distributive roll-a-dice game with a partner.
We continue the game after lunch, then students take the quiz.

standards: PA Career Education and Work Standard 13.3.11.B:
Demonstrate professional skills in the workplace, including appropriate work habits, organization, and time management.
essential_questions: Why is staying organized important?
How can staying organized help me succeed in school?
How can using an agenda help me remember important tasks and events?
objectives: By the end of the lesson, students will be able to identify at least two reasons why staying organized is important and use an agenda or to-do list to record at least three tasks, assignments, or important events.
assessment: Formative Assessment
Students will:
Verbally identify one reason organization is important.
Identify one way an agenda can help them.
Identify at least two things they could record in an agenda.
Use their mini agenda to record at least three personal or school-related tasks/events.
Check PowerSchool/Canvas and add at least one upcoming or missing assignment, if applicable.
differentiation:   Provide information through multiple formats, including verbal explanations, visual examples, and hands-on practice.
  Provide students with a physical agenda while also demonstrating digital options.
  Provide additional processing time and repeat or rephrase directions as needed.
  Model how to enter an assignment into an agenda before asking students to complete the task independently.
  Break the task into smaller steps: identify the task → identify the due date → write the task → check that it was recorded correctly.
  Provide one-on-one prompting or teacher assistance when needed.
  Allow students to use their existing classroom supports and IEP accommodations.
  Provide examples that are relevant to students' lives, such as homework, work schedules, sports, appointments, birthdays, and school activities.
  For students who do not regularly receive homework, allow them to record personal responsibilities, activities, or upcoming events.
environment: The lesson will follow the established classroom routines and behavioral expectations already used by the cooperating teacher.
At the beginning of the lesson, students will be informed of the learning objective and expectations for participation.
The teacher will:
Provide clear, concise directions.
Use a visual schedule/lesson sequence.
Provide positive reinforcement for participation and effort.
Use proximity and quiet redirection when needed.
Allow students appropriate processing time.
Provide choices when appropriate.
Maintain predictable transitions between activities.
Use students' established behavior supports and IEP accommodations.
Maintain a respectful and supportive classroom environment.
prior_knowledge: Ask students what they have used to stay organized so far throughout school
They have been taught to use binders and folders to keep papers in one spot
They get schedules at the beginning of the year so that they know where they are going and what time they need to be there
Ask them where they typically find assignments (canvas, powerschool)
vocabulary: Agenda: A personal list of tasks or events that need to be completed/remembered
Organization: arranging or planning things in a logical order (by putting them into a schedule, agenda, etc.)
To-do list: A list of tasks that need to be completed.
Calendar: A tool used to keep track of dates, events, and deadlines.
Due date: The date something needs to be completed or turned in.
sequence: Allow students to get settled and review the visual schedule for the lesson.
Introduce the lesson objective: "Today we are going to learn how staying organized can help us in school and after high school."
Display the question: "Why is staying organized important?"
Allow students to share their ideas verbally.
Discuss how organization can help students remember responsibilities, reduce stress, manage their time, and complete tasks on time.
Display the question: "How can an agenda help me stay organized?"
Allow students to share their ideas.
Show video on Keeping an Agenda
Explain that an agenda can be used to record assignments, due dates, tests, events, work schedules, appointments, and other important information.
Model how to take a sample assignment and record it in an agenda.
Ask students what information should be included when writing an assignment in an agenda.
Introduce four organizational tools:
To-do lists
Agenda books
Calendars
Online scheduling/planning resources
Discuss when and how each tool can be useful.
Ask students which organizational tool they think would work best for them and why.
Provide each student with a mini agenda.
Give students several sample tasks/events and have them practice recording them in their agenda.
Have students check PowerSchool/Canvas for upcoming or missing assignments.
Have students record appropriate assignments or responsibilities in their agenda.
Circulate and provide prompts, feedback, and assistance as needed.
Ask students to review their agenda and check that they have included the necessary information.
Have students share one thing they plan to use their agenda for.
closure: Review why keeping an agenda can help the students stay organized and get their work done on time, or help them remember any special dates or events
Allow them to use the rest of the time to check PowerSchool to see if they have any missing or upcoming assignments that they can work on for the rest of class
Encourage them to write down anything they did not complete in a to do list or agenda

objectives: Students will identify at least two reasons why keeping an email inbox organized is important.
Students will identify whether an email should be deleted, replied to, or acted upon when given common school/work-related examples.
Students will identify at least two strategies for maintaining an organized email inbox.
Given a school-based email scenario and a template/checklist, students will compose an organized email containing the necessary information, with support as needed.
Students will use a checklist to review an email before sending it.

Students will share when they can delete emails or reply to emails

Checklists to ensure students are not missing any steps (subject line, proof reading, etc)
