prior_knowledge: Begin with Slide 1, 'Staying Organized: Managing Your Email.' Ask students what they know about email, what they use it for, and how they currently organize their inbox. Connect the lesson to school, work, college/training programs, and everyday life. Explain that students will learn a repeatable routine for managing emails they receive and sending organized emails themselves.
materials: Printed email templates with word banks
vocabulary: Email – An electronic message.
Inbox – The place where received emails are stored.
Reply – To send a response to an email.
Delete – To remove an email that is no longer needed.
Spam – Unwanted or potentially harmful email.
Action – Something you need to do because of information in an email.
sequence: 1. Introduction / Prior Knowledge – 3 minutes: Display the title slide. Ask what students know about email and how they currently organize emails. Introduce the lesson goal.

2. Why Email Organization Matters – 5–7 minutes: Use Slide 2. Allow students to answer before explaining. Discuss classwork, schedule changes, meetings, RAMS time, job interviews, work schedules, and other important communication. Ask what could happen if an important email is missed.

3. How to Keep Email Organized – 5 minutes: Use Slide 3. Discuss deleting unnecessary emails, starring important messages, creating folders when useful, and writing down actions that need to be completed.
4. Introduce the Three Choices – 3 minutes: Use Slide 4. Introduce DELETE, REPLY, and TAKE ACTION. Explain that some emails may require more than one step.

5. When to Delete – 3 minutes: Use Slide 5. Discuss old/unneeded emails, spam, advertisements, and emails related to completed tasks. Emphasize that important information should not be deleted just to make the inbox smaller.

6. When to Reply – 3 minutes: Use Slide 6. Discuss responding when someone asks a question, needs confirmation, or when the student has a follow-up question. Explain that not every email needs a reply.
7. When to Take Action – 3 minutes: Use Slide 7. Discuss completing/turning something in, adding a date to a calendar, getting something signed, bringing something in, or completing another task.
8. Guided Practice – 6–8 minutes: Use Slides 8–11. Read each example aloud and allow students to decide whether they should reply, delete, or take action. Ask students to explain their reasoning.

9. Transition to Sending Emails – 1–2 minutes: Explain that staying organized also means managing emails students send. Introduce the student-led communication checklist, word bank, and late-work email template.

10. Student-Led Communication Emails – 3 minutes: Review the checklist. Discuss including a greeting, purpose, important information, questions, appropriate language, name, and checking the recipient before sending.

11. Email Word Bank and Template – 3 minutes: Explain how the word bank provides phrases for greetings, explaining why they are emailing, asking questions, and closing. Model how the late-work template can be used to tell a teacher that an assignment has been submitted.
Writing the email: 10 minutes: allow students to use templates and write their student led communication emails to their case managers/parents
closure: 3–5 minutes: Review DELETE, REPLY, and TAKE ACTION. Ask students to explain one reason email organization is important and one strategy they can use. Complete the exit ticket (verbally)
Closure:

Review the three main email decisions: DELETE when an email is no longer needed, REPLY when someone needs an answer or confirmation, and TAKE ACTION when the email requires the student to do something. Reinforce that students can also use checklists, word banks, templates, calendars, and folders as organizational supports.
Exit Ticket (verbal answers):
1. Name one reason it is important to keep your email organized.
2. What should you do if someone emails you asking a question?
3. What should you do if an email tells you to complete a form?
4. Name one strategy you can use to keep your email organized.
5. What is one thing you should check before sending an email?

standards: PA Career Education and Work Standards (effective July 1, 2026): 13.3.11.A — Evaluate personal attitudes and work habits that support career retention and advancement; 13.2.9-12.E — Evaluate time and project management strategies and their application to both personal and work situations.
essential_questions: What executive functioning skills do I use well, and which skills are areas I can improve?
objectives: Complete the Executive Functioning (EF) self-assessment on pages 6–8 of the provided ESS Executive Functioning Packet.
Rate and reflect on current executive functioning skills using the rating system provided in the packet.
Identify at least one executive functioning strength and one skill that could be improved.
assessment: Formative: teacher observation during the check-in, whole-group engagement, and quiz completion; questioning during discussion. Product evidence: completed EF quiz/self-rating on pages 6–8 and a brief verbal or written reflection identifying one strength and one area for growth.
differentiation: Provide the packet digitally or on paper; read directions aloud and clarify unfamiliar vocabulary without changing the intended self-rating. Chunk pages into smaller sections and provide one item at a time as needed. Allow students to respond verbally, point to choices, type, or use assistive technology. Provide extended time and frequent check-ins. Use a visual agenda and explicit modeling. Students ready for enrichment can identify a specific school/work situation in which improving one skill would help.
environment: Begin with the established daily check-in routine. Display a visual agenda and learning target. Review expectations: participate respectfully, answer honestly, and remember that the self-assessment is for identifying strengths and growth areas, not for getting a 'right' or 'wrong' score. Circulate during independent work, offer quiet redirection, and provide breaks when needed.
prior_knowledge: Connect to students’ existing routines by asking: 'What is one thing you do every day at school that helps you stay on track?' Briefly explain that executive functioning skills include planning, organization, self-monitoring, and managing tasks. Preview that today's quiz is a chance to notice current strengths and areas for growth.
materials: Daily check-in form; ESS Executive Functioning Packet, pages 6–8; pencils; computers/tablets if using a digital copy; projector/display; optional highlighters or sticky notes.
vocabulary: Executive functioning; self-assessment; self-reflection; organization; planning; self-monitoring; time management; task completion; strength; growth area.
sequence: 0–5 min — Daily check-in: Students complete the established daily check-in. Teacher briefly reviews any immediate needs and reminds students of the objective.
5–20 min — Whole-group engagement: Prompt students to name or identify examples of executive functioning skills they use at school. Teacher records examples and connects them to the lesson.
20-25 min — Introduce the lesson: Explain that students will complete an EF self-assessment and that honest answers are more useful than answers they think the teacher wants.

25-55 min — EF quiz/self-rating: Students complete pages 6–8 of the ESS Executive Functioning Packet. Teacher models how to interpret the rating scale and circulates to clarify directions and provide individualized support.

55-60 min — Review and reflection: Students review their responses and identify one area they feel confident about and one area they would like to improve. Students may share verbally, write, or type.
60-65 min — Individual teacher check-ins: Teacher briefly conferences with students to connect a growth area to a real school situation.
65-75 min — Transition/cleanup: Students turn in or save their completed work and prepare for dismissal.
closure: Students complete: 'One executive functioning skill I am proud of is ___, and one skill I want to work on is ___.' Preview that the class will use self-awareness to examine situations that can make it harder to stay regulated and successful.

standards: PA Career Education and Work Standards (effective July 1, 2026): 13.3.11.A — Evaluate personal attitudes and work habits that support career retention and advancement. PA Career Ready Skills: Self-Awareness and Self-Management — recognize feelings and respond effectively to challenges.
essential_questions: How can knowing my triggers help me choose a strategy before a situation becomes harder to manage?
objectives: Define a trigger as something that can cause a sudden emotional response.
Identify personal situations or events that may lead to irritation, upset, anger, sadness, or another strong emotional response.
Rank three common triggers by frequency or intensity and identify a strategy that may help in a school setting.
assessment: Formative: responses during the whole-group discussion, teacher questioning, and observation of student participation. Product evidence: completed trigger list with a top-three ranking and at least one appropriate school-based strategy for the highest-priority trigger.
differentiation: Normalize a range of emotions while maintaining the expectation that students are responsible for their actions. Offer examples and non-personal hypothetical situations so students can participate without disclosing sensitive information. Allow students to write, type, select from choices, or respond verbally. Provide a partially completed organizer, sentence starters, visual strategy choices, and private teacher support. Students ready for enrichment may identify multiple strategies and explain when each might be useful.
environment: Use a calm, predictable structure and remind students that sharing is optional. Establish a respectful discussion norm: no laughing at, judging, or repeating another student's personal information. Students may pass or use a hypothetical example. Teacher models neutral language and focuses on problem-solving rather than blame.
prior_knowledge: Ask students to recall yesterday's idea of identifying strengths and areas for growth. Introduce the idea that self-awareness also includes noticing situations that make it harder to use our skills. Give a neutral example, such as being asked to stop a preferred activity unexpectedly, and ask what feelings or actions might occur.
materials: Daily check-in form; trigger/strategy graphic organizer or paper; projector/display; pencils/computers; optional emotion scale or visual feelings chart; strategy choice cards.
vocabulary: Trigger, emotion, behavior, irritation, upset, strategy, coping strategy, self-management, intensity, frequency
sequence: 0–5 min — Daily check-in: Students complete the routine. Teacher briefly identifies any classroom needs that may affect participation.

5–20 min — Group engagement activity: Complete a short, low-risk activity about emotions or self-management, such as matching common situations with possible feelings. Emphasize that different people can have different reactions to the same event.

20-30 min — Direct instruction: Explain that triggers are events or situations that can lead to a sudden emotional response. Reinforce: emotions are not 'bad' or 'wrong,' but students remain responsible for how they respond or act.
30-35 min — Model: Teacher models a hypothetical trigger, identifies the feeling/response, and demonstrates choosing a strategy.
35-45 min — Independent reflection: Students list situations that can make them irritated, upset, angry, sad, or otherwise emotionally activated. Students may use personal or hypothetical examples.
45-55 min — Prioritize: Students identify their top three triggers based on how often they occur or how strongly they affect them. The highest-priority trigger is labeled #1.

55-65 min — Strategy planning: Next to the #1 trigger, students identify what they typically experience and one strategy they can use at school. Teacher conferences and helps students choose realistic strategies.
65–75 min — Share/transition: Volunteers share a general strategy, not a personal trigger. Students clean up materials.
closure: Students complete: 'When I notice ___, I can try ___.' Reinforce that recognizing a trigger is a first step toward making a more intentional choice about a response. Preview that the next lesson will focus on meeting new people and starting conversations.

standards: PA Career Education and Work Standards (effective July 1, 2026): 13.2.9-12.B — Use professional etiquette and observe social protocols when communicating verbally, nonverbally, and in writing; 13.2.9-12.C — Demonstrate shared responsibility for collaborative work and the value of contributions made by team members with various perspectives.
essential_questions: How can I start a conversation, show interest, and end a conversation appropriately?
objectives: Identify at least two appropriate ways to start a conversation with someone new.
Practice asking a question, listening to the response, and using a follow-up statement or question.
Identify at least two behaviors that help conversations remain respectful and appropriate.
assessment: Formative: teacher observation during whole-group discussion and partner practice; questioning and feedback during role-play. Performance evidence: completed Student Profile and participation in a brief conversation practice using an appropriate greeting, question, listening response, and closing.
differentiation: Provide the Student Profile in paper and digital formats. Read choices aloud and allow students to select, write, type, or dictate responses. Provide visual conversation cards with sentence starters and examples. Pair students thoughtfully and allow practice with the teacher or a trusted adult if peer interaction is uncomfortable. Model both appropriate and inappropriate examples without singling out students. For enrichment, students can practice follow-up questions and adapting communication to a workplace setting.
environment: Use predictable partner routines and explicitly teach respectful boundaries. Students may choose a partner when appropriate or be assigned one. Establish that students do not need to disclose private information. Teacher monitors interactions, provides feedback, and redirects off-topic or inappropriate comments respectfully.
prior_knowledge: Ask: 'What makes it easier or harder to talk to someone you do not know?' Acknowledge that ice-breakers can feel uncomfortable but explain that they provide a structured way to find common interests. Connect the skill to school, community, employment, and other real-life settings.
materials: Daily check-in form, Student Profile handout, conversation starter/follow-up cards, projector/display, pencils/computers, optional whiteboard table or paper.
vocabulary: Conversation, introduction, commonality, active listening, follow-up question, interest, respectful, personal information, social protocol, workplace etiquette.
sequence: 0–5 min — Daily check-in: Students complete the routine and prepare materials.
5–20 min — Daily engagement activity: Brief partner or whole-group prompt about a favorite interest, activity, food, or entertainment choice.
20-30 min — Whole-group discussion: Explain why meeting new people can be challenging and why structured ice-breakers can help people find common interests.

30-40 min — Student Profile: Students complete the profile with information they are comfortable sharing: name, interests, favorite food/music, strengths, something they want to learn, favorite place, and something that makes them happy.

40-45 min — Teacher modeling: Model a short conversation: greeting → question → listening response → follow-up → closing. Highlight phrases such as 'That's cool,' 'I like that too,' and 'Tell me more about that.'

45-55 min — Partner practice: Students turn to a classmate and practice introducing themselves and asking questions from the profile. Teacher circulates, prompts students as needed, and gives specific feedback.

55-65 min — Whole-group reflection: Discuss what helps a conversation go well and what should generally be avoided, such as interrupting, asking overly personal questions, making rude comments, or sharing someone else's private information.
65-75 min — Closing practice: Each student identifies one conversation skill they can use again.
closure: Students state or select one skill they practiced: starting a conversation, asking a question, listening, showing interest, or ending a conversation. Preview that the next lesson will involve communicating with families and school staff through the weekly Student-Led Communication email.

standards: PA Career Education and Work Standards (effective July 1, 2026): 13.2.9-12.B — Use professional etiquette and observe social protocols when communicating verbally, nonverbally, and in writing; 13.3.11.A — Evaluate personal attitudes and work habits that support career retention and advancement.
essential_questions: How can I communicate about my progress in a clear, respectful, and responsible way?
objectives: Access PowerSchool and obtain a current screenshot of grades.
Locate the Student-Led Communication email and use Reply All to communicate with the appropriate recipients.
Write one thing the student is proud of and one area the student plans to work on, and attach/paste the grade screenshot.
Star the email thread so it can be located easily for future weekly check-ins.
assessment: Summative/product assessment: completed Student-Led Communication email. The weekly task is worth 5 points when all required components are completed on Thursday; 4 points when completed on the next school day after a reminder; 3 points when completed during the additional make-up day (typically Monday); after Monday, the assignment receives a zero according to the classroom procedure. Teacher checks for the required screenshot, Reply All, reflection statements, and starred thread.
differentiation: Provide the previously supplied email template and Canvas example. Use a projected model and complete each step one at a time. Provide a checklist and allow students to work from a printed or digital checklist. Support students with reading, typing, navigation, or organization needs while maintaining student ownership of the message. Allow speech-to-text or other approved assistive technology. For enrichment, students can independently review the tone, clarity, and completeness of their message before sending.
environment: Follow the established Thursday routine consistently. Display a visual checklist and model the process without displaying private student grades or email content. Remind students that the email is a school communication and should use respectful, school-appropriate language. Teacher circulates to provide navigation and writing support while encouraging independence.
prior_knowledge: Review Wednesday's focus on respectful communication and connect it to written communication. Ask: 'What makes an email to a teacher or family member different from a text to a friend?' Briefly identify professional tone, complete information, and appropriate recipients as key differences.
materials: Daily check-in form, Student computer, powerschool, gmail, student-led communication email template, grade screenshot, teacher checklist/rubric, projector display
vocabulary: Professional communication, Reply All, recipient, screenshot, reflection, progress, goal, tone, email thread, star.
sequence: 0–5 min — Daily check-in: Students complete the routine.
5–15min — Review objective and expectations: Explain that Thursday's task is a graded weekly communication routine designed to build independence and self-advocacy.

15-25 min — Teacher model: Demonstrate the process using a non-student example: open PowerSchool → view grades → take screenshot → open Gmail → find the Student-Led Communication email → select Reply All.
25-50 min — Student work time: Students complete the process independently as able. Teacher provides step-by-step prompts only when needed.
50-55 min — Write the reflection: Students state one thing they are proud of and one thing they plan to work on. Students may use the provided template and Canvas example.
55-60 min — Insert screenshot and proofread: Students paste the grade screenshot into the email and check that the message includes all required parts and uses appropriate language.
60-65 min — Send and star: Students send the completed email and click the star on the email thread so it is easy to find each week.
65-75 min — Teacher verification/closure: Teacher checks completion and gives immediate feedback or identifies the next step for students who need assistance.
closure: Students complete a quick checklist: 'I checked my grades; I wrote my reflection; I included my screenshot; I used Reply All; I starred the thread.' Reinforce that this routine builds independence in communicating about school progress.

standards: PA Career Education and Work Standards (effective July 1, 2026): 13.2.9-12.E — Evaluate time and project management strategies and their application to both personal and work situations; 13.3.11.A — Evaluate personal attitudes and work habits that support career retention and advancement.
essential_questions: How can an organization reset help me finish the week prepared for the next one?
objectives: Complete the daily Google Form check-in.
Review materials and identify unfinished schoolwork that needs attention.
Organize a backpack and/or locker using an appropriate system.
Participate appropriately in a structured choice activity after required tasks are complete.
assessment: Formative: teacher observation of chick-in completion, work review, organization behaviors, and student use of an organization system. Product evidence: completed check-in, completed or documented work tasks, and organized backpack/locker. Teacher may use a simple checklist to document independence and level of prompting.
differentiation: Provide a visual Friday checklist with tasks in order. Allow students to complete organization tasks one area at a time. Provide adult prompting, modeling, and organization support when included in the student's IEP or classroom plan. Offer sorting categories such as 'Keep,' 'Take Home,' 'Turn In,' and 'Needs Attention.' Allow alternative storage systems for students who have difficulty managing a backpack or locker. For enrichment, students can create a personal weekly organization routine or identify one change that would make next week easier.
environment: Use a predictable end-of-week routine: check-in - unfinished work - organization reset - choice activity. Establish clear criteria for moving to games: required academic and organization tasks must be completed or appropriately documented. Maintain a calm, positive environment and reinforce independence rather than speed.
prior_knowledge: Ask students to think about what happens when papers, assignments, or materials are difficult to find. Connect Friday's organization reset to Monday's self-assessment and the class's ongoing focus on executive functioning. Explain that organization is a habit that can make school and work responsibilities easier to manage

vocabulary: Organization, reset, unfinished work, priority, checklist, routine, materials, sort, organize, independent, responsibility.
sequence: 0–5 min — Daily Google Form check-in: Students complete the form and review the day's checklist.

5–15 min — Work completion check: Students review assignments, folders, digital work, and teacher directions. Teacher helps students identify what is finished, what is missing, and what needs to be completed or addressed.

15-50 min — Complete/organize: Students complete priority work when possible and/or organize materials needed for upcoming classes. Teacher uses a checklist and prompts students to work independently before providing more direct assistance.

50-55 min — Backpack/locker reset: Students organize their backpack and locker if applicable. Suggested categories include 'Keep at school,' 'Take home,' 'Turn in,' and 'Needs attention.' Teacher checks for a functional system rather than appearance alone.

55-70 min — Structured choice activity: Once required tasks are complete, students may choose from approved games and activities such as UNO, Monopoly, puzzles, LEGOs, or board games. Teacher observes cooperation, communication, and following classroom expectations.

lessons.title: Emotional Awareness

standards: PA Career Education and Work Standard 13.3.11.A: Analyze how personal beliefs, attitudes, and behaviors affect decision-making and interactions with others.
PA SEL Competency — Self-Awareness: Identify and label emotions; recognize how emotions influence behavior.
essential_questions: How does being aware of our emotions affect the way we respond to situations?
How can understanding our emotions help us manage them in healthy ways?
objectives: Students will be able to identify the emotion a person might feel in a given situation.
Students will be able to explain how noticing a feeling before reacting (emotional awareness) affects the way a person responds to a situation.
Students will be able to identify at least one calming/coping strategy to use when experiencing a strong emotion.
Students will be able to describe how a specific emotion (e.g., fear, anger, sadness) can serve a helpful purpose.
assessment: Verbal or nonverbal responses during the 'What Might They Do?' group situation activity
Active participation in the guided breathing/calming exercise
Completed Emotional Awareness worksheet (ways emotions can help us)
Completed 'How Might You Feel' worksheet
differentiation: Visual schedule posted and referenced throughout to support predictability
Concrete, literal framing of abstract ideas (e.g., 'Situation → Feeling → What I Do' chain, feelings thermometer/scale)
Option to pass or respond nonverbally (pointing, writing) during group discussion
Simplified worksheet version with fewer scenarios and sentence starters for the student in the life skills program
Extra processing time before being asked to respond aloud
Teacher modeling and think-alouds provided before independent worksheet work
environment: Visual schedule displayed and referenced at the start of class and during transitions
Consistent daily routine: check-in → daily engagement → group activity → direct instruction → independent worksheet → closure
Clear verbal and visual cues signal transitions between activities
Group discussion norms reinforced: one person talks at a time, 'pass' is always an option
Calm, low-pressure tone maintained, especially during emotional-awareness discussion
prior_knowledge: Students enter and complete their daily check-in using the visual schedule posted on the board.
Daily engagement activity (Wordle, Contexto, or a set game) to settle in and warm up.

Group activity — 'What Might They Do?': A situation is displayed on the board. Say: "I'm going to put a situation on the board. I want you to think, not about what emotion the person feels yet, but about what they might do in that moment. There's no wrong answer, we're just guessing together." Take several guesses per situation.

Ask: "If it's the same situation, why might two people react differently?" (Pause for guesses.) Say: "A lot of the time, it comes down to the feeling underneath the action. What someone feels affects what they do, even when they don't realize it's happening." This motivates today's focus on emotional awareness.
materials: Whiteboard/projector with visual schedule and situation prompts
Emotional Awareness worksheet (ways our emotions can help us)
vocabulary: Emotional awareness — noticing what you are feeling, especially before it turns into an action
Trigger — the situation or event that causes a feeling
Coping/calming strategy — a tool used to manage a strong feeling
React vs. respond — reacting automatically vs. pausing to choose an action
sequence: Introduce emotional awareness: "That's what we're focusing on today, not just what people do, but the feeling that's driving it. This is called emotional awareness, noticing what you're feeling, and noticing it before it turns into an action you didn't mean to do."

Explain why awareness matters: "Feelings happen fast, and sometimes we react before we even realize what we're feeling. But if you pause and notice 'hey, I'm feeling frustrated' or 'I'm feeling nervous,' that little bit of awareness gives you a moment to decide what to do next, instead of just reacting on autopilot." Note that this pause also gives you a chance to use a calming/coping strategy.

Introduce the idea that emotions have a purpose: "Big emotions don't always feel good, but even uncomfortable emotions are trying to help us in some way, they're giving us information. Today's worksheet is about figuring out what that information is, and how each emotion can actually work for us instead of against us."

Give examples before handing out the Emotional Awareness worksheet: Fear/Nervousness → keeps us safe or prepared ("If you feel nervous before a test, that's your brain telling you 'this matters, get ready.' That nervous feeling can actually push you to study or review your notes."); Anger/Frustration → signals something feels unfair or a boundary was crossed ("If you feel frustrated when a friend keeps interrupting you, that feeling is pointing out that something doesn't feel right, and it might be a signal to speak up or ask for space.")
Read through the Emotional Awareness worksheet instructions together and have students answer the question at the bottom.

Transition to the calming tool: "We talked about how being aware of how you are feeling can affect your actions: when you notice a feeling before you react, you get a chance to choose your response instead of just reacting automatically. But noticing a feeling is only the first step. Sometimes, especially with big feelings, frustration, anxiety, anger, noticing isn't enough on its own. You also need a way to actually calm that feeling down before you can think clearly and choose your next move. That's where having a tool comes in. One simple tool is a short breathing or calming exercise, something you can use anytime a feeling starts to feel like too much. Let's practice one right now, together, so it's already familiar for whenever you actually need it."
Play guided breathing/calming meditation video as a whole group.

Introduce independent practice: "Okay, now I want you to practice being aware of your emotions. You have a worksheet called 'How Might You Feel.' I want you to read through these scenarios and write down how you might feel in these situations. You don't have to write this part down, but I want you to think about what you might do to make yourself feel better in these situations or what your emotions in these situations mean."
Students work independently on the 'How Might You Feel' worksheet; circulate to support as needed.
closure: Students hand in both worksheets (Emotional Awareness and How Might You Feel).
Briefly recap the big idea: noticing a feeling gives you a chance to choose your response, and calming tools help when a feeling gets big.
Preview that tomorrow's lesson will continue building on these skills.
Students with time remaining work on any missing assignments.

lessons.title: Working in Groups

standards: PA SEL Competency — Relationship Skills: Use communication and social skills to interact effectively with others, including active listening, turn-taking, and staying on topic during group interactions.
PA Career Education and Work Standard 13.3.11.B: Analyze the importance of collaboration and group participation skills in school, work, and community settings.
essential_questions: Why is it important to be able to work well in groups?
What does working well in a group look like in school, at work, and in the community?
objectives: Students will identify key group-participation skills: listening, sharing ideas, not talking over others, and staying on topic.
Students will connect the conversation ball activity to real-life group work skills.
Students will identify examples of situations that require working in groups in school, at work, and in the community.
Students will share a personal experience related to working in a group.
assessment: Participation in the conversation ball activity, including turn-taking and responding to follow-up questions
Verbal identification of the group skills used during the activity
Participation in the discussion of school/work/community group examples
Sharing of a personal group-work experience
differentiation: Visual schedule posted and referenced for predictability
Conversation ball provides a physical, turn-based cue so students know when it's their turn to speak
Teacher models follow-up questions to scaffold conversational engagement for students who need support extending their answers
Concrete, real-world examples (school/work/community) used to make the group-work concept concrete rather than abstract
Option to pass during personal sharing
Choice of homework or a game during work time to accommodate individual pacing/needs
environment: Visual schedule displayed and referenced at the start of class
Consistent daily routine: check-in → Wordle → conversation ball → group skills lesson → discussion → work time
Group norms reinforced during the conversation ball: one person talks at a time, listen to whoever is holding the ball, ask follow-up questions
Positive reinforcement for using group skills (listening, staying on topic) during discussion
prior_knowledge: (0-5 min) Students enter, follow the schedule on the board, and complete their daily check-in.
(5-15 min) Wordle completed together as a group.
materials: Daily check-in sheet or digital tool
Discussion prompts/examples for school, work, and community group scenarios
Homework materials and/or games (Uno, Monopoly, etc.) for end-of-period work time
vocabulary: Listening — paying attention to what someone else is saying
Staying on topic — saying something that connects to what's already being discussed
Collaboration — working together with others toward a shared goal
sequence: (15-25 min) Group engagement activity: pass around the conversation ball. Each student answers the question their thumb lands on; everyone gets a turn. The class asks follow-up questions to each person's answer.

(25-35 min) Transition into the lesson: explain that the conversation ball activity was practice for working in groups, since students listened, shared their ideas, didn't talk over their classmates, and stayed on topic.
(35-45 min) Review examples of when working in groups is needed: in school, at work, and in the community.
(45-55 min) Students share a personal experience of a time they needed to work in a group.

lessons.short_version_text:
Wednesday: Working in Groups
Daily Check-In
Warm-up: wordle, contexto, sets game
Group activity: Pass the conversation ball
make sure everyone is listening to one another and taking turns
"We just did a fun warm-up getting to know each other a little better, but that conversation ball actually connects to something really important we're going to talk about today: working in groups.
No matter what you choose to do after high school, whether you go to college, go straight into a job, or live on your own in the community, you are going to need to work in groups and collaborate with other people. This isn't just a 'school skill.' It shows up everywhere:
In school — group projects, class discussions, working with classmates, sports teams, clubs
At work — teaming up with coworkers, taking direction from a boss, working alongside customers or clients
In the community — living with roommates, working with neighbors, being part of clubs, teams, or community groups
So today, we're going to focus on four key things that help us work well in a group, no matter which setting we're in:
 Listen first — look toward the person talking, and don't start talking over them
 Wait for a turn — let one person talk at a time
 Stay on topic — say something that connects to what's already being discussed
 Share, don't take over — say your piece, then let someone else have a turn
you actually already practiced these four skills without even realizing it, during the conversation ball warm-up. Every time you waited for the ball, listened to the person holding it, and then added something that connected to what they said, you were using these exact group skills.
That's the goal for today: to notice these skills when we're using them, and to start thinking about how you'll use them not just here in class, but in whatever comes next after high school: college, a job, or life in your community."
"Let's make this a little more real, here are some examples of what working in a group might actually look like in each of these settings.
In school:
Working with a partner or small group on a class project
Being part of a class discussion where everyone takes turns sharing ideas
Working with a lab partner in science class
At work:
Splitting up tasks with coworkers to get a job done faster
Listening to feedback or instructions from a supervisor
Working as a team during a busy shift — like at a restaurant, store, or warehouse
In the community:
Living with a roommate and figuring out chores or shared space together
Being part of a team, club, or volunteer group
Working with neighbors on something like a block cleanup or a shared project
Notice something ,in every single one of these examples, you'd need to use our four skills: listening first, waiting for your turn, staying on topic, and sharing without taking over. It doesn't matter if you're in a classroom, on a job site, or just living your life in your community , these skills go with you everywhere."

lessons.title: Mindfulness & Breaking Down Tasks

standards: PA SEL Competency — Self-Management: Manage stress and use organizational/task-planning strategies (e.g., mindfulness, breaking tasks into steps) to reach goals.

essential_questions: How can mindfulness strategies help us clear our minds and calm our thoughts?
How can breaking a task into smaller steps make it more manageable?

Students will verbally break down a familiar task (making a PB&J, choosing an outfit) into manageable steps.
Students will identify the purpose and benefits of breaking tasks into smaller steps.
Students will identify at least two strategies for breaking down tasks (e.g., small due dates, timers, one step at a time, checklists).
Students will independently break down a task of their choice using a Canvas quick check.

Verbal participation in the group task-breakdown activity (PB&J / outfit)

Choice of warm-up activity to support engagement

Teacher support available during the Canvas quick check as needed

lessons.title: Triggers & Coping Strategies
lessons.subject_line: Executive Skills / Emotional Awareness & Coping Strategies
lessons.text:
Gwynedd Mercy University-School of Business & Education
(Must be used for each lesson observed by University Supervisor)
Lesson Plan Framework

Subject Area: Executive Skills / Emotional Awareness & Coping Strategies		Grade Level: 9–12

Student Name: Grace Dittman


PA Standard(s):
PA Health, Safety and Physical Education 10.3.9.C / 10.3.12.C: recognize conflict situations and identify strategies to avoid or resolve them, including walking away and adult intervention. The lesson also supports emotional wellness, self-awareness, and appropriate coping responses. Pennsylvania's current Health, Safety and Physical Education standards remain the adopted standards while revisions are under review.
Students will consider and reflect on throughout the lesson:
What am I feeling? What is causing the feeling? Is this a big or small problem? Can the trigger be removed? Do I need to take a step away?
Success Criteria
Students will complete at least four of five trigger/coping-strategy examples on the worksheet with an appropriate strategy. Students may use words, short phrases, examples, or another approved communication method.
Differentiated Instruction
Provide visual supports and the five-question decision sequence; read directions aloud; chunk the worksheet; provide sentence starters/word banks; allow students to choose from a visual list of coping strategies; provide extended processing time; model examples before independent work; allow verbal, written, typed, or other approved response formats; check in individually as needed. Students needing additional challenge may explain why a strategy fits a particular trigger or identify more than one possible strategy.
Domain II: Classroom Environment
Students enter and begin the established daily check-in routine. The class follows predictable transitions: check-in, group game, video/discussion, direct instruction, worksheet practice, and independent work.
Classroom/Behavior Management Plan & Routines
Maintain a calm, respectful environment. Students may participate verbally or through an approved alternative communication method. Students are reminded that personal examples may be kept private and that they may use a hypothetical school-appropriate example instead. Teacher provides positive reinforcement, proximity, redirection, and private check-ins when needed. During independent work, students may transition to missing assignments after completing the coping-strategy worksheet.
Activate Prior Knowledge/Motivation
Connect the lesson to the previously taught emotional awareness lesson. Explain: “Today we're going to take that one step further and use our emotional awareness to figure out what to actually do when a strong feeling comes up.” Students will recall that recognizing and naming emotions is the first step toward responding appropriately.
Vocabulary
Trigger; coping strategy; emotion/feeling; emotional awareness; problem size; remove the trigger; step away; calm down; response.

Sequence 
Daily check in (3-5 minutes)
Do group activity (wordle,contexto, set game, etc) on the board (5-8 minutes)
Introduce todays topic “identifying coping strategies” (1 minute)
Show video on triggers and coping strategies (5 minutes)
Discuss emotional awareness (last week’s lesson) and let students know we will be talking about the next steps (choosing a coping strategy after they have identified their emotions) (5 minutes)
Discussion: "Today we're going to take that one step further and use our emotional awareness to figure out what to actually do when a strong feeling comes up.
This slide gives us a simple set of questions to walk through whenever something's bothering us. Let's go through them one at a time.
First: What are you feeling?
Before we can decide what to do, we have to name the feeling. Are you frustrated? Nervous? Angry? Disappointed? Just naming it already gives us a little bit of control over it.
Second: What is causing this feeling?
Every feeling has a trigger — something that happened right before it. Maybe a friend said something that upset you, or an assignment felt too hard, or your plans got changed last minute. Figuring out the 'why' helps us figure out what to do next.
Third: Is this a big problem or a small problem?
Not every problem needs the same response. A small problem — like someone cutting in line — might just need a deep breath. A big problem — like a real conflict with a friend — might need a bigger strategy, or even an adult's help. Sizing up the problem helps us pick the right tool for it.
Fourth: Can the trigger be removed?
Sometimes we actually can change the situation. If a loud noise is bothering you, you might be able to move somewhere quieter. If a certain conversation is stressing you out, you might be able to politely step out of it. Not every trigger can be removed — but it's always worth asking.
Fifth: Do I need to take a step away?
Sometimes the best thing we can do is give ourselves some space — a short break, a walk, a few minutes alone — before we respond to anything. Stepping away isn't giving up, it's giving yourself time to calm down so you can think clearly.
So next time something's bothering you, try walking through these five questions in your head. They won't solve every problem, but they'll help you figure out what kind of coping strategy actually fits the moment." (10 minutes)
Introduce worksheet: identify a trigger and find a coping strategy that can go with it to help you stay calm: we will go over 2 examples together and the students will finish the last three on their own (10 minutes)
They can work on missing assignments when the worksheet is complete
Closure / Teacher Reflection Notes
Closure: Students will name or select one coping strategy they could use in a future situation. Teacher summarizes the connection between emotional awareness, identifying a trigger, sizing the problem, and selecting a coping strategy.
Monitoring for Understanding: Teacher listens for accurate identification of feelings/triggers during discussion and checks whether worksheet strategies are reasonable and safe for the situation described.
Possible Next Step: Use student worksheet responses to identify common coping strategies that may need additional practice. Future lessons can focus on practicing selected strategies in realistic school situations.
Overall Assessment: The lesson will be evaluated based on student participation, discussion responses, successful completion of the worksheet, and the appropriateness of selected coping strategies. The teacher will adjust the amount of modeling or guided practice based on student independence.

Standards note: PA Health, Safety and Physical Education standards were referenced for conflict-resolution and safe-response skills.

standards: PA SEL Competency — Relationship Skills: Use communication and social skills to interact effectively with others, including active listening and turn-taking in conversation.
essential_questions: What does it look like to actively listen and keep a conversation going?
How can I use conversation skills to build and maintain connections with others?
objectives: Students will be able to identify at least two behaviors of active listening (e.g., eye contact, nodding, asking follow-up questions).
Students will be able to practice starting and maintaining a conversation using a shared prompt.
Students will be able to take turns respectfully during a group conversation activity.
assessment: Participation in the group discussion on active listening/conversation skills
Teacher observation during Conversation Jenga: turn-taking, engagement, use of active listening behaviors
differentiation: Visual list/anchor chart of active listening behaviors posted for reference during the activity
Option to pass on a question and choose a different block
Sentence starters available for students who need support beginning a response
Small, consistent group sizes for Conversation Jenga to reduce social pressure
Extra processing time allowed before a student is expected to respond
environment: Consistent daily routine: warm-up → check-in → group discussion → Conversation Jenga → closure
Clear group norms posted for Conversation Jenga: one person talks at a time, listen while others answer, 'pass' is always allowed
Small groups arranged ahead of time to support comfortable participation
prior_knowledge: (0-10 min) Warm-up: Wordle, Contexto, or the Sets game as a whole group.
(10-15 min) Daily check-in.
materials: Daily check-in sheet or digital tool
Conversation Jenga tower(s) with conversation-starter questions on each block
vocabulary: Active listening — fully focusing on and responding to what someone is saying
Turn-taking — waiting for your turn to speak and letting others speak without interrupting
Follow-up question — a question that shows interest and keeps a conversation going
sequence: (15-25 min) Group discussion: introduce active listening and conversation skills. Discuss what active listening looks like (eye contact, nodding, asking follow-up questions) and why it matters for keeping a conversation going. Model a short example conversation together, pointing out these behaviors.

(25-55 min) Conversation Jenga: in small groups, students take turns pulling a block, reading the question aloud, and answering it while practicing active listening (e.g., one other group member asks a follow-up question before the next turn). Teacher circulates to support group and reinforce active listening behaviors.
(55-85 min) Catch-up work time: students use remaining class time to complete missing assignments or other classwork, with teacher support available.
closure: (85-90 min) Groups clean up their Jenga towers. Briefly recap: what's one active listening behavior you used or noticed today? Preview that tomorrow will continue practicing conversation/social skills.

lessons.title: Prioritizing Tasks
lessons.text:
Monday Prioritizing Tasks
Daily Check-In
Group Question: What is your favorite Halloween movie?
Mindfulness
Introduce prioritizing tasks lesson 
What does it mean to prioritize tasks? 
Let students answer with their ideas
Prioritizing tasks means to arrange or complete tasks in the order of importance and urgency (more important tasks come first)
What tasks should you be prioritizing?
Let students answer with their ideas (let them known its okay if they don't know)
We will talk more about what tasks should be prioritized first
Show prioritizing tasks video (start at 1:30 min)
The video mentions splitting tasks into “urgent” and “not urgent”, how do you decide what is urgent vs what is not? 
Urgent: the due date is soon, it is worth a lot of points (tests, projects), it is a meeting/interview that is soon
Prioritizing tasks slide:
Again, decide what is urgent and what is important
Consider what your goal is: 
It is important to complete your goals, however it is also important to decide whether or not your goal can wait, is there something you need to complete first?
Examples from the video: the girl’s goal was to finish her video game, but she recognized that she needed to pack for her trip that was the next day before she could finish her video game
Next Slide: BIG, medium, small tasks
Split your tasks into BIG, medium, and small tasks
Big tasks come FIRST: exams, big projects, job interviews
Medium tasks come second, they should still get done, but consider doing them after your big tasks: daily homework, club meetings
Small tasks: you should still be doing small tasks and fun activities, but try to complete your important work first because these things are not a priority. 
Hand out prioritizing work worksheet, students can fill in their tasks in the calendar and answer the question below based on the lesson and their big vs small tasks
Give time to finish missing assignments

lessons.title: Dealing with Disappointment
lessons.text:
Tuesday: Dealing with Disappointment
Daily Check-In
What’s your favorite Halloween candy? 
Group activity: Healthy Self Expression
Read sheet (on board)
Have the students come up and color in the boxes with healthy self expression and explain why they filled that box in 
Ask students in what ways do they express their feelings (there is no pressure for them to share this out loud)
Introduce lesson: dealing with disappointment with video
Show video
When plans change, it can be disappointing, disappointment can feel like anger, it is important that we express our feelings in a healthy way when we feel like this 
Dealing with Disappointment worksheet
Read it together and then ask students to fill out at the bottom a time they were disappointed by something (they can share if they'd like)
Read next slide about how disappointments help us grow
Remind students of our perseverance lesson: it is important to not give up when we feel badly about something, continuing during a hard or disappointing time helps us grow
Have students fill out the “Disappointments help us grow” paper: What advice would you give a friend dealing with disappointment? 
Read summary slide
Its okay to feel upset when there are disappointments
Staying flexible helps you accept and adapt to unexpected changes
Disappointment can feel like anger, it is important that you recognize how you are feeling and chose a healthy way to express yourself
Choose a coping mechanism that helps you: taking a walk, using a fidget, talking to a friend/teacher
Good things can come out of disappointment:
Maybe a fun trip gets canceled, but another one that is even more fun gets scheduled for a different time
Work on missing assignments

lessons.title: Being Perceived as Friendly
lessons.source: ESS/weeks 8+9/Lesson Plans/10_21-10_28 Being Perceived as Friendly.docx
lessons.text:
Wednesday: Being Perceived as Friendly
Daily Check-in
Ask students what traits they look for in a friend
Allow them to answer verbally
Do you think being kind is important in friendships?
What are some benefits of being friendly?
Allow students to answer verbally
Next Slide: Read the reasons why being friendly is important
People will want to be your friend
People like kindness in friends
It makes people more likely to help you
If you are kind to people, they typically want to be kind back, people do not want to help you if you are mean to them
It is a good skill to have at a job
Being kind can help you make a good first impression, a boss will see that you can be kind to both customers and coworkers
It makes you feel better
When you are kind to people, it releases serotonin which is a chemical hormone that makes you feel happy
Gives you more opportunities
People may offer you jobs, trips, invites to events/parties
Look at Being perceived as Friendly worksheet: read it together as a class 
“This worksheet talks about ways you can be perceived as friendly if you don't know where to start”
There is nothing to fill out on this worksheet, students should just have it and we can talk about it as a class 
Sometimes saying the right things can take thought. 
Make sure you think about if what you are about to say is kind and respectful 
Is it an inside thought or a thought you should say out loud
Inside vs outside thoughts
Hand out cards and have students answer whether they are inside or outside thoughts
Are they kind, can the person fix the problem right away, is it helpful 
Have students put their cards on the board in the think it or say it column 
Ask students what they can do to be perceived as friendly, and answer as a quick check on Canvas
Work on missing assignments

standards: PA Career Education and Work Standard 13.3.11.B: Analyze the role of self-advocacy and professional communication skills in personal and academic success.
essential_questions: How do I write a clear, professional email to communicate with important people in my life?
Why is self-advocacy, sharing my strengths and areas I want to grow in, important for my success?
objectives: Students will write a student-led email to their case manager, parent(s), and ESS teacher using the provided template.
Students will include a subject line, greeting, body (one strength and one growth area), and a screenshot of their PowerSchool grades in their email.
Students will use a word bank to compose an appropriate greeting and closing.
Students will proofread their email using a provided checklist before sending.
Students will organize their inbox by deleting old emails or replying to any that need a response.
assessment: Completed, sent email checked against template requirements (subject line, greeting, body with strength/growth area, grade screenshot)
Completed proofreading checklist
Completed inbox organization checklist
Progress on missing assignments during remaining work time
differentiation: Physical copy and online/digital copy of the email template both provided so students can use whichever format supports them best
Word bank provided for greeting and closing language
Proofreading checklist scaffolds self-editing (subject line present, greeting/closing used, screenshot attached, etc.)
Inbox organization checklist scaffolds the closing routine (delete old emails, reply to any needing a response)
Teacher/aide support available for typing, taking the PowerSchool screenshot, or navigating email
environment: Visual schedule displayed showing today's routine
Consistent daily routine: check-in → warm-up → student-led email → inbox organization → missing work time
Clear expectations reviewed for professional/appropriate use of school email
Positive reinforcement for completing the self-advocacy email independently
prior_knowledge: (0-5 min) Students enter and complete their daily check-in.
(5-20 min) Warm-up group activity: Wordle, Contexto, or the Sets game.
materials: Daily check-in sheet or digital tool
Physical copy of the student-led email template
Online/digital copy of the student-led email template
Devices with access to student email (starred email to reply all to) and PowerSchool
vocabulary: Self-advocacy — speaking up for your own needs and progress
Subject line — a short summary of what an email is about
Greeting/closing — the opening and ending of an email
Proofread — checking your work carefully for mistakes before submitting
sequence: (20-50 min) Students draft their student-led email using the physical or online template, replying all to their starred email. Email includes: a subject line, a greeting (using the word bank), a body with one thing they are proud of and one thing they want to work on, and a screenshot of their current PowerSchool grades.
(50-60 min) Students proofread their email using the checklist (subject line, greeting/closing, screenshot attached, etc.) and send it.
(60-70 min) Students use the inbox organization checklist to delete old emails or reply to any that need a response.
(70-90 min) Students work on any missing assignments
closure: Quick check-out: did you send your email? How do you feel about the strength and growth area you shared?
Preview that tomorrow will follow the same daily routine.

standards: PA Career Education and Work Standard 13.3.11.B: Analyze the role of personal management skills (e.g., organization, responsibility, self-advocacy) in achieving personal and academic success.

Note: verify alignment with individual students' IEP goals related to executive functioning/organization, since this is a recurring routine-based skill-building period rather than new academic content.
essential_questions: How does staying organized and on top of responsibilities help me succeed in and out of school?
What strategies can I use to manage my time, my materials, and my responsibilities independently?
objectives: Students will complete a daily check-in routine.
Students will identify whether they have missing assignments and use class time to complete them.
Students will organize their binder, backpack, and/or locker using an organizational system when materials need it.
Students will demonstrate appropriate, responsible use of free-choice time once responsibilities are complete.
assessment: Completion of daily check-in
Participation in the group engagement activity
Missing-work completion log/tracking
Binder/backpack/locker organization checklist
Teacher observation of on-task behavior and appropriate choices during work/free-choice time
differentiation: Visual schedule and routine chart posted and referenced daily for predictability
Individualized, up-to-date missing-assignment list provided for each student
Choice of organizational tools/systems (folders, color-coding, checklists, digital planner) based on student need
Clear, posted expectations and modeled examples for appropriate free-choice activities (voice level, sharing, cleanup)
Teacher check-ins throughout the period to support self-monitoring and decision-making about which task to prioritize
Task-card or checklist system showing the sequence of steps (check-in → group activity → missing work check → organize/work/free choice) for students who benefit from concrete sequencing
environment: Visual schedule/routine posted and used daily so the structure is predictable
Consistent daily routine: check-in → group engagement activity → missing work check → organize/work/free choice time → closure
Positive reinforcement for completing responsibilities (check-in, missing work, organization) before accessing free-choice time
Established norms for free-choice/game time: respectful volume, sharing materials, cleaning up before the period ends
Teacher circulates throughout independent work time to check in, redirect, and support decision-making
prior_knowledge: (0-5 min) Students enter, review the visual schedule, and complete their daily check-in.
(5-20 min) Whole-group engagement activity: Wordle, Contexto, or the Sets game, played and discussed together to start class with a shared, low-pressure warm-up.
materials: Daily check-in sheet or digital tool
Organizational supplies: folders, binders, labels, organization checklists
Board/card games for free-choice time (Uno, Monopoly, etc.)
vocabulary: Self-management — the ability to monitor and take responsibility for your own tasks and behavior
Prioritize — deciding what needs to be done first
Organizational system — a consistent method for keeping materials in order (e.g., folders, labels, checklists)
Accountability — following through on responsibilities
sequence: (20-25 min) Missing work check: students individually review their missing-assignment list to determine whether they have work to complete.
(25-80 min) Work time, based on individual need:
If a student has missing work, they use this time to complete it, with teacher support available.
If a student is caught up but their binder, backpack, or locker needs organizing, they use this time to organize using the checklist/system provided.
If a student has completed both missing work and organization, they may choose an appropriate game (Uno, Monopoly, etc.) to play independently or with a peer.
(80-88 min) Work time continues; teacher circulates to check progress, redirect as needed, and confirm students have appropriately completed responsibilities before choosing free time.
closure: Students clean up any games or materials used during the period.
Quick check-out: each student shares one thing they accomplished today (verbally or on an exit slip) — completed an assignment, organized materials, etc.
Preview that tomorrow will follow the same daily routine.
